passage: The monsoon had flooded the ground floor of the school, so exams were shifted to the library, crowded and noisy. Anjali sat at the corner table, her hands no longer shaking the way they had a month ago. The boy who started the rumour had been called to the principal, and the school had followed its rules; nobody knew exactly what, and nobody needed to. In the class group, someone had posted: "Before you forward anything, remember what happened." Now, between papers, Thomas slid her a pen because hers had leaked, and Chinmay shared his umbrella for the walk to the bus. Anjali laughed at one of Chinmay's bad jokes. It surprised her. She hadn't laughed at school in weeks.

qa.q: Why were the exams shifted to the library?
qa.a: The monsoon had flooded the ground floor of the school.

qa.q: What does Anjali's surprise at her own laugh suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she is healing and feeling safe again, after weeks of not laughing at school.

qa.q: What helped Anjali recover at this stage?
qa.a: The school handled the source under its rules, classmates learned to think before forwarding, and friends like Thomas and Chinmay stayed close in small ways.

qa.q: How might Thomas and Chinmay feel about their friendship with Anjali now?
qa.a: They probably feel closer to her, having stood by her through a hard time, and glad to see her laugh again.

grounding: It shows the school dealing with the source under its rules, classmates rethinking forwarding, and the target recovering with friends who became closer.

passage: Devika's mother dropped her at the school gate in Hyderabad on Monday, and for the first time in weeks Devika didn't ask to be picked up early. The two boys who had made the fake account had been dealt with by the school, and the class had had a long talk with the counsellor about forwarding. Some classmates had even messaged Devika to say sorry for sharing it. "I didn't think," one wrote. At lunch, Manjula saved her a seat as usual, and the others squeezed in. They were planning Manjula's birthday. "You're doing the decorations, Devika," someone said. She nodded, smiling. Manjula nudged her. "See? Told you it would get better." Devika nudged her back.

qa.q: How can you tell Devika is feeling safer at school?

passage:
It's been two months since the rumour about me and the stolen phone, and I finally feel like myself again.

The school handled it. The girl who started it had to meet the principal with her parents, and she was suspended for a week. There was a whole assembly about how forwarding a message is a choice, and that choice has harm attached. Some people who'd forwarded it came up to me afterwards and said sorry. Not all of them.

What I remember most isn't the punishment, though. It's Santosh. On the worst day, when I was crying in the corridor, he stood next to me and told people to move on. He walked me to the counsellor's room. He sat with me at lunch for two weeks when no one else would.

We were just classmates before. Now he's the person I call first.

— Elizabeth

qa.q: How long was the girl who started the rumour suspended?
qa.a: For a week.

qa.q: How does Elizabeth feel about Santosh now?
qa.a: Elizabeth feels deeply grateful and close to Santosh, now the first person Elizabeth calls.

qa.q: What did the school's response teach the group?
qa.a: That forwarding is a choice with harm attached, shown through the principal's action and the assembly.

qa.q: How might Santosh have felt standing next to Elizabeth in the corridor?
qa.a: He was probably nervous about standing out but determined to support Elizabeth.

grounding: Elizabeth recovers after her school deals with a rumour's source and teaches that forwarding causes harm, and she grows close to the friend who stood by her.

passage:
Counsellor's note, final session with Afreen

Six weeks ago Afreen came to me after a false rumour about her spread through the Class 9 chats. She was barely eating and had missed four days of school.

Since then, the school has acted. The student who started it met the principal with parents and faced consequences under our code. The class held a session on forwarding: every forward is a decision that can hurt someone. Two students came to apologise to Afreen in person.

Today Afreen laughed twice in our session. She told me she has rejoined the quiz team. She talked most about her friends Nazia and Liz, who sat with her at lunch every day of that first bad week. "We were friends before," she said. "Now they're family."

She will check in with me monthly. I am closing weekly sessions.

— Sunaina Ma'am

qa.q: How many days of school had Afreen missed?
qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: How does Afreen seem to feel in the final session?
qa.a: She seems much better, laughing and hopeful, and grateful to Nazia and Liz.

qa.q: What combination helped Afreen recover?
qa.a: The school's consequences for the source, the class session on forwarding, apologies, counselling support, and friends who stood by her.

qa.q: How might Nazia and Liz see their friendship with Afreen now?
qa.a: They probably feel closer too, and proud they chose to sit with her when others didn't.

grounding: A counsellor's note shows the school acting on the source of a rumour, the group learning forwarding causes harm, and Afreen recovering with friends who stood by her.

passage:
Thursday night
Today felt almost normal. The principal spoke to the whole of Class 9 in assembly: the girl who made the fake post about me has been suspended for three days under the school rules, and the four who forwarded it have to do sessions with the counsellor. She didn't say my name, and I was grateful for that. Ms D'Souza said, "Forwarding is a choice. Every forward is a push." For once nobody looked at me.
At lunch Swati saved my seat like she has every day for three weeks, and Harleen and Mehr came to sit too. Three weeks ago I thought I'd never want to walk down that corridor again.
Tonight Mummy called me her brave girl, and I let myself believe it. I still check the group sometimes. But less. Gurpreet, you're getting there.

qa.q: What happened to the girl who made the fake post?
qa.a: She has been suspended for three days under the school rules.

qa.q: What does 'Today felt almost normal' suggest about how Gurpreet is feeling?
qa.a: Gurpreet feels relieved and steadier, supported by friends and the school after three weeks of dreading the corridor.

qa.q: What did the school do that helped both the target and the group?
qa.a: It applied its rules to the source, sent those who forwarded to the counsellor, kept Gurpreet's name out of assembly, and taught that every forward is a choice.

qa.q: How might Swati see these three weeks?
qa.a: Swati has saved Gurpreet's seat every day, so she probably feels loyal and closer, and glad to see things turning.

grounding: Shows a school dealing with the source of a rumour under its rules while the target recovers with support and loyal friends grow closer.
